title: When 'Evidence-Based' Starts Meaning Everything... and Nothing
author: ReadWriteJen
summary: Jen (ReadWriteJen) argues that 'research-based' and 'evidence-based' -- two phrases now used almost interchangeably in literacy education -- describe genuinely different relationships to research, and conflating them is a serious professional hazard for teachers navigating programme decisions. 'Research-based' is the modest claim: a programme drew on existing research during development but has not been independently tested or shown to improve outcomes for children. 'Evidence-based' is the stronger claim: a programme has been evaluated through rigorous designs -- RCTs, longitudinal studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses -- and demonstrated to produce better results. The article maps the hierarchy of evidence from medicine (systematic reviews at the top; testimonials at the bottom) onto literacy, arguing teachers need to locate any given claim on this hierarchy rather than accepting the label at face value. Holly Lane's 'snake oil' diagnosis identifies how programmes simulate scientific authority through neuroscience terminology, selective citations, and confident marketing even when the instructional evidence is weak or developer-generated. The article closes with a practical set of diagnostic questions -- Has this been independently evaluated? By developers or external researchers? Compared to what? -- reframing professional responsibility as informed critical consumption rather than statistical expertise.
points: 'Research-based' means only that research informed a programme's development -- it makes no claim about independent evaluation or demonstrated effectiveness, yet it functions in literacy discourse as an all-purpose defence, claiming a relationship with research without being held accountable to any particular evidentiary standard.

The evidence hierarchy (systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top, then RCTs, longitudinal studies, case studies, and testimonials at the bottom) should function as a practical map for teachers: 'it worked in our school' is not the same as evidence, and conflating anecdote with research is precisely where the field runs into difficulty.

Phonics instruction is genuinely evidence-based in the fullest sense -- converging RCTs, systematic reviews, and national inquiries across three countries (National Reading Panel 2000, Rose Review 2006, Rowe 2005) -- but this does not mean every programme marketed as phonics is equally effective; each programme's independent evaluation record is the decisive question.

Holly Lane's 'snake oil' diagnosis: literacy programmes can appear highly scientific through neuroscience terminology, selective citations, and confident marketing even when the instructional evidence base is weak or limited to developer-generated studies -- the packaging can be extraordinarily convincing.

Professional responsibility is not statistical expertise but critical interrogation: Has this programme been independently evaluated? By the developers or by external researchers? With students similar to ours? Compared to what alternative? Does the confidence of the marketing match the strength of the research?
quotes: Research-based is the more modest claim. A programme described as research-based may have drawn on existing research findings during its development, but drawing on research is not the same as being shown to work. A literacy programme might reference research on oral language, motivation, or the value of discussion... while still having no independent evidence that the programme itself improves reading outcomes.

In practice, research-based has become one of the most overused and least scrutinised phrases in literacy education. It is often applied so broadly, and with so little consistency, that it can function as a kind of all-purpose defence, a way of claiming a relationship with research without being held accountable to any particular standard of evidence.

The language of research can sound extremely persuasive, particularly when wrapped in polished presentations, confident delivery, and references to 'brain science'. Part of teachers' professional responsibility is learning to pause and ask: what kind of evidence actually sits underneath this claim? How strong is it? And does the confidence of the messaging match the quality of the evidence being presented?

The conclusion that systematic, explicit phonics instruction works is not the same thing as saying that every programme marketed as a phonics programme is equally effective. Some phonics programmes have been independently evaluated through rigorous research and produce reliable outcomes for children. Others are more accurately described as research-based.

Snake oil relies on persuasive marketing, compelling testimonials, and grand promises rather than robust proof. Literacy education is not immune to this. Programmes can appear highly scientific through the use of neuroscience terminology, selective citations, and references to 'brain-based learning', even where the evidential foundations are weak, incomplete, or contested.

'It worked in our school' is not the same thing as evidence that something works, and conflating the two is where the field has repeatedly run into difficulty. Professional experience matters. But we need to be precise about what kind of claim is being made and what level of evidence supports it.

Reading is not simply another school subject. It is the gateway through which children access almost everything else in education. Teachers who understand what these terms actually mean, and who feel comfortable to ask what kind of evidence is really on the table, are better placed to make decisions that genuinely serve the children in front of them.
